description: We're a team of passionate innovators interested in space exploration, AI, engineering, and technology. Our goal is to tackle real-world challenges using NASA's data, creative thinking, and practical solutions. We're looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in programming, AI/ML, engineering, data science, UI/UX, or design. Experience is welcome, but curiosity, creativity, and teamwork matter most. Let's combine our strengths and build something meaningful!
summary:
We are Team Astralis. Our Lunar Landing Site Navigator addresses the lunar South Pole's power and Earth-communication constraints. Our novel contribution is a mission-specific search that discovers candidate landing patches beyond preset NASA sites by combining solar-elevation-derived energy, continuous Earth visibility, and slopes below 10° over 100 metres.

For a landing on 25 December 2026 at 00:00 UTC and a seven-day (168-hour) mission, we identified Patch 1 at 84.0215°S, 10.0372°W as the best balanced sampled candidate: 4.06 kWh/m² of modeled solar energy, 156.6 hours of continuous Earth view, and a 0.14° slope. Alternative patches prioritize full-mission communication or maximum solar energy. Changing the landing date or mission window changes the recommendation.

Using NASA/JPL ephemerides and LRO/LOLA terrain, we turn scientific data into inspectable decisions. Seamless Orbit–Moon Map–Surface transitions and first-person walking connect each result to its terrain. Progressive detail lets students learn intuitively while technical users inspect timelines, assumptions, comparisons, and exported data.
details:
Our discovery: novel candidate sites for specific mission windows

We are Team Astralis, creators of Lunar Landing Site Navigator. The lunar South Pole offers valuable exploration opportunities, but low solar elevation, crater shadows, uneven terrain, and changing Earth visibility make a landing location meaningful only in the context of a mission's timing. Our main contribution is a novel, mission-specific landing-patch finder beyond the preset NASA and catalog sites. It searches 6,685 sampled terrain patches across 84°S–90°S and combines modeled solar energy, uninterrupted Earth-view windows, and a slope screen.

For 25 December 2026 at 00:00 UTC through 1 January 2027 at 00:00 UTC, we discovered Patch 1 (84.0215°S, 10.0372°W) as the best balanced candidate among the sampled patches under our model. The recorded seven-day result gives 4.06 kWh/m² of solar energy, approximately 24.2 W/m² average power over the entire mission, 156.6 continuous hours of Earth view (93% of the 168-hour mission), and a 0.14° terrain slope. This is a computationally identified landing candidate for that particular window; it is not a claim that the coordinates were previously unknown or that NASA has certified the site.

The same mission also produces different recommendations for different priorities: Patch 569 provides 168 continuous hours of Earth view (100%) with 3.42 kWh/m² of modeled energy; Patch 961 maximizes modeled energy at 5.37 kWh/m² with 105.6 continuous Earth-view hours. Patch 1 balances those trade-offs. These are actual rounded results shown in our demonstration, not invented example values. Users can change the UTC landing date and mission duration and run the search again.

How the novel search works

NASA LOLA slope and roughness products supply a representative low-slope sample from each 4 km search cell. The default screen is less than 10 degrees over a 100-metre baseline, following the cited Artemis reference; it is degrees, not percent grade. The app then evaluates each eligible patch over the selected mission window.

  • Solar elevation and energy: sunlight duration alone does not express power output. For our assumed horizontal panel, unblocked power is proportional to max(0, sin(solar elevation)), with a Sun-distance correction and fixed 20% efficiency. Terrain blockage and total eclipses set direct power to zero. We integrate this power over the full mission to obtain kWh/m²; average power is energy divided by mission duration. We do not substitute the arithmetic mean of elevation angles for average power.
  • Earth visibility: the app reports total Earth-view percentage, timelines, gaps, and the longest uninterrupted Earth-view interval. A long continuous window can matter more than the same number of disconnected hours.
  • Three transparent priorities: Best Communications seeks full-mission Earth visibility and then the highest energy; Best Solar Power prioritizes integrated energy subject to the selected requirements; Best Balance uses the geometric mean of normalized energy and the fraction of the mission covered by the longest continuous Earth-view window. The slope screen applies before ranking.

From a recommendation to an explorable surface

Our shared viewer moves seamlessly from an orbital Sun–Earth–Moon view to the Moon map and into a first-person surface view where users can walk and look around. The selected location and time stay connected across the transition. Sun/Earth directions, terrain horizons, shadow layers, solar-power layers, and visibility timelines help explain why a candidate ranks well. Generated foreground rocks and fine dust are illustrative; they do not enter the scientific calculations.

The separate Trade-off Explorer supports the existing catalog of 39 landing and study locations, including preset NASA regions. It provides mission presets, date comparisons, synchronized South Pole maps, progressively deeper detail, a trade-off plot, raw data and CSV export, and JPL query links. Its catalog comparisons complement the novel patch search. A gazetteer adds 9,087 named lunar features. Students can begin with visual comparisons and walking; technical users can inspect the numbers, methods, and limitations step by step.

NASA data and implementation

NASA/JPL SPICE inputs include DE440s ephemerides, lunar orientation and frame kernels, and leap seconds. Python preprocessing produces apparent Sun/Earth vectors at 15-minute intervals for surface calculations and hourly geometric positions for the orbital display, with bundled coverage from January 2024 through December 2030. NASA LRO/LOLA elevations provide terrain horizons and shadow geometry. The adjusted South Pole DEM, slope, and roughness products drive the patch analysis; finer LOLA and LROC stereo terrain support local surface inspection. NASA long-term illumination is a separate contextual layer, not a replacement for the selected mission dates. NASA SVS imagery supplies attributed Moon, Earth, and Sun displays.

The application uses HTML, CSS, native JavaScript modules, WebGL/GLSL, Canvas, and Web Workers. Python, NumPy, Rasterio/GDAL, SpiceyPy, pyproj, and Pillow support data preparation and on-demand terrain. Git/GitHub support collaboration; Node.js and Playwright support numerical and browser checks. Core calculations use bundled scientific data without a generative-AI API call. A modern browser and ordinary computer are sufficient; additional on-demand terrain detail needs internet access.

Impact, validation, and limits

We aim to make early South Pole mission planning understandable and reproducible: discover promising mission-specific candidates, compare the power/communications trade-off, and immediately inspect the environment behind the recommendation. The handbook records an independent JPL Horizons comparison, and automated checks cover geometry, ranking, data integrity, controls, and browser workflows.

These are preliminary screening results. Earth-center visibility is geometric opportunity, not a radio-link guarantee. The panel estimate omits actual hardware orientation, storage, thermal effects, dust/degradation losses, and partial solar-disk blockage. Candidate horizons use 3-degree bearing samples; patch ranking uses 15-minute steps through 30 days and two-hour steps for longer windows, so brief interruptions can be missed. A low 100-metre-baseline slope does not resolve every boulder or footpad hazard. Surface-rendering detail does not imply the same resolution in every ranking calculation. Our contribution is the mission-dependent search and explanation, not a universal NASA landing-safety certification.

Team work and SI disclosure

Team Astralis developed the project concept, priorities, and integrated experience. Deb prepared the integration and v1.5.0 release; vnk11 contributed the Trade-off Explorer. OpenAI Codex assisted with research, interpretation, code, debugging, data-processing scripts, documentation, and submission wording. OpenAI ImageGen produced the identified concept/hero artwork and dust material. Numerical celestial positions and measured terrain come from the credited scientific sources.

The 30-second demo uses our actual application recording, AI-assisted HyperFrames/GSAP editing and annotations, ElevenLabs synthetic Roger narration and sound effects, and original locally synthesized music. Its visible AI-assisted/synthetic-audio label and metadata disclose this use. No commercial music sample was used. External scientific inputs, imagery, methods, fonts, and tools are credited in the resource fields and repository source register.
